chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan and Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ubaydullah ibn Abdullah al-Dihqan, from Durust al-Wasiti, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) entered the mosque, and there was a group who had encircled a man. So he said: 'What is this?' It was said: 'An Allama (great scholar).' He said: 'And what is an Allama?' They said to him: 'The most knowledgeable of the people regarding the lineages of the Arabs, their battles, the days of the Jahiliyya, and Arab poetry.' So the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'That is a knowledge which neither harms the one who is ignorant of it, nor benefits the one who knows it.'

Then the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Indeed, knowledge is only of three types: a decisive verse (from the Quran), or a just obligation, or an established Sunnah — and whatever is besides these is superfluous.'

key_terms.آيَة مُحْكَمَة: A decisive/firm verse — a Quranic verse with clear and unambiguous meaning
key_terms.سُنَّة قَائِمَة: An established Sunnah — a prophetic practice firmly grounded in tradition
key_terms.عَلَّامَة: Allama — a title for an exceptionally learned person, here applied ironically to one with only worldly knowledge
key_terms.فَرِيضَة عَادِلَة: A just obligation — a religious duty established with fairness and equity
key_terms.فَضْل: Superfluous/excess — in this context, knowledge that is beyond and outside the three essential categories

ai.seo_question: What are the three types of true knowledge according to the Prophet in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam al-Kazim (AS) narrates a hadith in which the Prophet (SAWW) encounters a crowd gathered around an 'Allama' — a man praised for his extensive knowledge of Arab genealogy, tribal battles, pre-Islamic history, and poetry. The Prophet dismisses this as a knowledge of no religious utility, and then defines true knowledge as comprising three categories: the Quran's decisive verses (establishing creed and ethics), just legal obligations (fiqh), and the established Sunnah (prophetic practice). This tripartite definition became a foundational principle in Shia epistemology, distinguishing knowledge that serves salvation from knowledge that is merely worldly erudition.
